content: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) is a condition characterized by inflammation affecting various parts of the body, including the heart, blood vessels, kidneys, digestive system, brain, skin, or eyes. Evidence suggests that children with MIS-C often have antibodies against COVID-19, indicating a prior COVID-19 infection. The clinical presentation of MIS-C resembles Kawasaki disease, which is why it is sometimes referred to as a Kawasaki-like disease. It also shares features with staphylococcal and streptococcal toxic shock syndromes, bacterial sepsis, and macrophage activation syndromes. Classification of Disease Severity in MIS-C: 1. Mild Disease: Children in this category require minimal or no respiratory support. They exhibit minimal or no organ injury. They are normotensive and do not meet the criteria for ICU admission. 2. Severe Disease: These children have significant oxygen requirements, such as high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC), BiPAP, or mechanical ventilation. They may have mild to severe organ injury, including ventricular dysfunction. They require vasoactive support and meet the criteria for ICU admission. Pathophysiology: The exact mechanism underlying MIS-C remains unclear. However, the following hypotheses have been proposed: A lag time between COVID-19 infection and the onset of MIS-C suggests the possibility of antibody-dependent enhancement. Coronaviruses are known to block type I and type III interferons, leading to a delayed cytokine response. In children with a high initial viral load or an inadequate immune response, this delay may result in a cytokine storm, causing MIS-C. MIS-C often presents with gastrointestinal symptoms, suggesting that the virus may replicate predominantly in the gastrointestinal tract. Differential Diagnosis: MIS-C should be differentiated from the following conditions: Bacterial sepsis Staphylococcal and streptococcal toxic shock syndromes Kawasaki disease Epidemiology and Demographics: A study of 186 children with MIS-C revealed that hospitalization rates were 12% between March 16 and April 15, and 88% between April 16 and May 20. 80% of these children required intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and 20% required mechanical ventilation. 4% of the children required extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). The mortality rate was 2%. Age Distribution: <1 year: 7% 1–4 years: 28% 5–9 years: 25% 10–14 years: 24% 15–20 years: 16% Comorbidities: Clinically diagnosed obesity: 8% BMI-based obesity: 29% Cardiovascular disease: 3% Respiratory disease: 18% Autoimmune or immunocompromising conditions: 5% Organ System Involvement: 71% of children had involvement of at least four organ systems. The most commonly affected systems were: Gastrointestinal: 92% Cardiovascular: 80% Hematologic: 76% Mucocutaneous: 74% Pulmonary: 70% Complications: Severe complications of MIS-C include: Myocardial infarction Cardiac failure or arrest Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) Hypervolemia Acute kidney injury Peritonitis Thrombotic complications Diagnosis: Diagnostic Criteria: Age 0–19 years with fever lasting more than 3 days. Presence of at least two of the following: Rash or bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis or mucocutaneous inflammation (oral, hands, or feet). Hypotension or shock. Myocardial dysfunction, pericarditis, valvulitis, or coronary abnormalities (e.g., echocardiographic findings or elevated troponin/NT-proBNP). Evidence of coagulopathy (e.g., prolonged PT, PTT, or elevated D-dimers). Acute gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal pain). Elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., ESR, C-reactive protein, or procalcitonin). No other identifiable microbial cause of inflammation (e.g., bacterial sepsis or toxic shock syndromes). Evidence of COVID-19 infection (e.g. Signs and Symptoms: Fever lasting 24 hours or longer. Gastrointestinal symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain. Skin rash. Conjunctivitis. Mucocutaneous changes: redness or swelling of the lips, tongue, hands, or feet. Neurological symptoms: lethargy, confusion, headache, syncope. Lymphadenopathy. Emergency Warning Signs: Difficulty breathing. Chest pain. New-onset confusion. Lethargy. Cyanosis. Severe abdominal pain. Physical Examination and Laboratory Findings: Blood tests may reveal lymphopenia, neutrophilia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Abnormal fibrinogen levels, hypoalbuminemia, and elevated creatine kinase (CK), LDH, and triglycerides are common. Inflammatory biomarkers such as ESR, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin are elevated. Cardiac biomarkers, including troponins (cTnI, cTnT) and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), are often elevated. Radiological Findings: Imaging studies may show evidence of inflammation or organ dysfunction. Blood cultures and viral PCR tests are used to rule out other potential causes. Treatment: Medical Therapy: All children with MIS-C are treated as suspected COVID-19 cases. Mild to moderate cases are managed supportively. Supplemental oxygen is provided for children with low oxygen saturation. Fluid resuscitation is performed cautiously to maintain euvolemia and avoid hypervolemia. Anti-inflammatory treatments, such as intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) with or without corticosteroids, have shown good efficacy. Aspirin is recommended for its antiplatelet effects in all MIS-C patients. Anakinra or tocilizumab may be considered in cases where fever persists for more than 24 hours after initial treatment with steroids or IVIG, or in moderate to severe cases. Empiric antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, ceftriaxone, clindamycin) are administered in cases of suspected community-acquired shock until cultures are negative for 48 hours. Prevention:
